newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan farmers want budget to remove tax snags.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan farmers want budget to remove tax snags.

text.p: Pakistani farmers are hoping that Friday's 1997/98 (July-June) government budget will iron out tax anomalies and promote interest rate cuts.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif raised support prices for wheat, rice and oilseeds in April to try to boost the vital agriculture sector, expected to grow a dismal 0.7 percent this fiscal year, compared to a targeted five percent.

He also ended sales tax on government-certified seeds, promised a cut in duties on locally-made tractors and other agricultural machinery, and reduced import duty on used and reconditioned harvestors to 10 percent from 35 percent.
But farmers, who have long resisted the imposition of agricultural income tax, say tax distortions and high interest rates are still crippling their ability to increase production.
"A water sprinkler can be imported duty-free, but its tyres are heavily taxed," said Siddiq Akbar Bukhari, a Multan-based farmer and member of the Farmers Association of Pakistan (FAP).
Various taxes on farm machinery, insecticide and fertiliser imports, along with local, provincial and federal taxes on farms and crops, distort the whole agriculture system, said Bukhari.

He said interest rates of up to 24 percent a year made it hard for small farmers -- 44 percent own less than 12.5 acres, 32 percent less than 25 acres and 16 percent less than 50 acres -- to obtain funds.
Qamar-uz-Zaman Shah, president of the Sindh Chamber of Agriculture, said big landlords took most of the low-interest farm loans due to complicated procedures for obtaining them.
"The finance minister should break the vicious circle, lower interest rates and simplify the procedure in the budget."
Shah called for a cut in customs duty on imported tractors, now selling for 450,000 rupees ($11,113) instead of 374,000 a few months ago due to rupee depreciation and customs duty.
"Now is the time to cut output costs and raise yields as acreage cannot be increased due to water-logging and salinity which makes 10 percent of the land infertile yearly," he said.
He said holdings of up to 25 acres should be exempt from farm income tax, newly levied by provinces at varying rates.
Analysts say recent increases in support prices should boost wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane crops next year.
"We expect a 10 percent rise in wheat output," Tariq Sadiq, chairman of the Food and Agriculture Committee of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters.
This year's wheat harvest is expected to be similar to last year's 17.1 million tonnes, well below the targeted 18 million and estimated consumption of 20 million tonnes.

Sadiq said rice production would rise five percent above this year's target of 4.2 million tonnes, against last year's 3.9 million tonnes. Cotton output was likely to rise 14 percent to 10 million 375-lb bales from 8.78 million in 1996/97.
Vegoil dealers say any increase in cotton production would boost cottonseed oil production, reducing demand for imported palm oil from Malaysia and soyoil from North and South America.
Pakistan Sugar Mills Association Secretary General Khadim Ali Qazilbash forecast a 25 percent rise in sugar production to 3.0 million tonnes from an estimated 2.38 million in 1996/97.
Pakistan spent $1.248 billion on food imports in the first 10 months of 1996/97, against $1.484 in the year-ago period.
